big_idea: Remarkable results come from tiny, 1% improvements repeated consistently over time, and lasting behavior change happens when you build systems and shift your identity rather than chase one-off goals through willpower alone.

tool.label: The four laws of behavior change
tool.text: To build a good habit: make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy, make it satisfying. To break a bad habit, invert each law: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult, and unsatisfying.
tool.note: The four laws map directly onto the four stages of the habit loop: cue, craving, response, reward.

ideas.title: Identity-based habits
ideas.text: Change your self-image before your outcomes. Every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become, so real change starts at the identity level, not the outcome level.

ideas.title: The habit loop
ideas.text: Cue, craving, response, and reward form a neurological feedback loop that automates behavior. Understanding each stage lets you deliberately redesign a habit.

ideas.title: Environment design
ideas.text: Your surroundings act as an invisible hand shaping behavior. Rearranging cues, visible versus hidden, is often more effective than relying on discipline.

ideas.title: The plateau of latent potential
ideas.text: Results lag effort, like an ice cube that shows nothing until a threshold is crossed. That's why people quit right before a breakthrough.

ideas.title: Habit stacking and implementation intentions
ideas.text: Pairing a new habit with an existing routine, and stating a specific time and location, dramatically increases follow-through.

ideas.title: The two-minute rule
ideas.text: Scale any new habit down to something that takes two minutes or less, to defeat the inertia of getting started.

try_it: Do a habit scorecard: list your daily routine and mark each behavior plus, minus, or neutral to build awareness of automatic behaviors.
Write one implementation intention: I will [behavior] at [time] in [location].
Make one bad-habit cue invisible, like moving a distracting app off your home screen, and one good-habit cue obvious.
Apply the two-minute rule to a habit you've been avoiding by shrinking it to a starter version.
